// Original teaching notes aligned to publisher chapter numbers. An Astra unit map is
// a topic-coverage index, so it does not assign textbook chapters to a course section.
export const openStaxChapterRows=[
  [1,'The Study of Life','scientific reasoning;scientific method;experimental controls;technical replication',
    'A hypothesis is a testable explanation. A prediction says what you expect to measure if it holds. A comparison group gives you a baseline for judging whether the factor you changed explains the result.',
    'To study whether light affects bean growth, change light exposure and measure height over the same period. Keep the water and soil similar across groups.',
    'What is the response variable in this experiment?','The bean plants’ measured growth is the response. The amount of light is the variable the experimenter changes.'],
  [2,'The Chemical Foundation of Life','water and life;hydrogen bonding;water polarity;buffering;carbon skeleton;chemical bonds',
    'Electron arrangement helps explain how atoms bond. Polar covalent bonds and the bent shape of water make water molecules attract one another. Carbon can form four covalent bonds and build skeletons with different shapes and properties.',
    'A buffer takes up added H⁺ or supplies H⁺ when the solution loses it. This keeps pH steadier within the buffer’s useful range.',
    'How does pH 5 compare with pH 6?','A pH of 5 has ten times the hydrogen ion activity of pH 6. Each whole pH step represents a factor of ten.'],
  [3,'Biological Macromolecules','macromolecule;macromolecules;biomolecules;monomer;polymer;dehydration synthesis;peptide bonds',
    'A monomer is a building unit. A polymer links many units in a chain. Sugars can form polysaccharides, amino acids form polypeptides, and nucleotides form nucleic acids. Most lipids are assembled in other ways.',
    'A peptide bond links amino acids. In a simplified condensation model, forming the bond releases the components of water. Hydrolysis uses water to break a bond.',
    'Which type of building unit makes up a protein?','Amino acids. Their side chains help determine how the chain folds and what the protein can do.'],
  [4,'Cell Structure','cell structure;organelles;microscopy;field diameter;endomembrane system;prokaryotic vs eukaryotic',
    'Cells share a membrane, genetic material, cytosol, and ribosomes. Eukaryotic cells also compartmentalize tasks in a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles. A microscope’s resolution determines whether close details can be seen separately.',
    'A protein made for export usually enters the rough ER, passes through the Golgi, and travels in a vesicle to the cell surface.',
    'What does increasing magnification accomplish if resolution stays unchanged?','It makes the existing image larger. Details too close for the microscope to resolve still merge together.'],
  [5,'Structure and Function of Plasma Membranes','membrane transport;plasma membrane;potato osmosis;active transport;facilitated diffusion;plasmolysis',
    'The membrane is a flexible phospholipid bilayer with proteins. Passive transport follows a gradient. Primary active transport can use ATP to move a substance against its electrochemical gradient. Osmosis describes net water movement across a membrane.',
    'A potato sample that gains mass in a sugar solution has taken up net water. Comparing percentage changes works better than comparing grams alone if samples start at different masses.',
    'Does a channel have to use ATP to help a substance cross downhill?','No. A channel can make passage easier while the gradient determines the net direction. This is facilitated diffusion.'],
  [6,'Metabolism','enzyme activity;metabolism;endoergonic;endergonic;exergonic;activation energy;denaturation;enzyme saturation',
    'Metabolism is the sum of a cell’s reactions. Exergonic reactions release free energy and can drive endergonic reactions. Enzymes help reactions run faster by lowering the activation barrier. The free-energy change stays the same.',
    'At high substrate concentrations, many enzyme active sites are already occupied. Adding more substrate then gives little extra increase in rate.',
    'On a free-energy diagram, what changes when a catalyst is added?','The peak between reactants and products drops. The starting and ending energy levels stay fixed.'],
  [7,'Cellular Respiration','cellular respiration;fermentation;glycolysis;citric acid cycle;oxidative phosphorylation;atp yield',
    'Glycolysis splits glucose. Pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle pass more electrons to carriers. In aerobic respiration, ATP synthase uses a proton gradient made by electron transport. Oxygen accepts electrons at the end of the chain.',
    'Fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue. Glycolysis provides a net 2 ATP per glucose in that pathway.',
    'Do NADH molecules make ATP directly?','NADH gives electrons to the transport chain. That helps build the proton gradient used by ATP synthase.'],
  [8,'Photosynthesis','photosynthesis;calvin cycle;photosystem;light dependent reactions;carbon fixation',
    'The light reactions use light energy to produce ATP and NADPH. Splitting water releases O₂. In the stroma, the Calvin cycle uses ATP and NADPH to turn CO₂ into organic carbon.',
    'Trace three inputs separately. Light supplies energy, water supplies replacement electrons, and CO₂ supplies carbon for the sugars.',
    'The oxygen released by photosynthesis comes from which molecule?','Water. When photosystem II takes electrons from water, molecular oxygen is released.'],
  [9,'Cell Communication','cell signaling;cell communication;signal transduction;receptors;phosphorylation cascade',
    'A signal changes a cell only if the cell can receive and respond to it. Receptor activation starts a series of internal events called signal transduction. The result might be a change in enzyme activity or gene expression.',
    'Two cells can encounter the same signal yet respond differently if only one has the right receptor or downstream proteins.',
    'What happens if a cell lacks the receptor needed for a signal?','That receptor pathway cannot start, so the signal will not trigger the response through it.'],
  [10,'Cell Reproduction','mitosis;interphase;cell cycle;cytokinesis;mitotic index;chromosome counting',
    'Interphase includes G₁, DNA copying in S phase, and G₂. During mitosis, chromosomes condense, spindle attachments form, chromosomes line up, sister chromatids separate, and daughter nuclei form. Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.',
    'A cell with four chromosomes has four replicated chromosomes and eight chromatids after S phase. Count joined sisters as one chromosome until they separate.',
    'What directly separates in mitotic anaphase?','Sister chromatids split and move toward opposite poles. The separated chromatids are then counted as daughter chromosomes.'],
  [11,'Meiosis and Sexual Reproduction','meiosis;haploid and diploid;crossing over;reduction division;homologous chromosomes',
    'Meiosis starts after one round of DNA copying and proceeds through two divisions. Homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis I, reducing the number of chromosome sets. Sister chromatids separate in meiosis II.',
    'Crossing over between nonsister chromatids in prophase I creates new combinations of alleles on a chromosome.',
    'A diploid species has 2n = 8. How many chromosomes are in a typical gamete?','Four. One member of each of the four homologous pairs is represented in a typical gamete.'],
  [12,'Mendel’s Experiments and Heredity','mendelian inheritance;punnett square;dominance;segregation;mendel experiments',
    'A diploid individual typically has two alleles for a gene. During gamete formation the two alleles separate. A Punnett square combines possible gametes to show probabilities for individual offspring.',
    'For Aa × Aa, the four outcome boxes give AA, Aa, Aa, and aa. With complete dominance, three boxes show the dominant phenotype.',
    'What percentage of offspring are expected to be Aa in this cross?','50%. Two of four equally likely outcomes carry one A and one a.'],
  [13,'Modern Understandings of Inheritance','genetic linkage;x linked inheritance;sex linked inheritance;recombination;nondisjunction',
    'Chromosomes carry multiple genes. Genes near one another on the same chromosome often travel together, while crossing over can separate them. Sex-linked traits follow the inheritance of the chromosome that carries the gene.',
    'New allele combinations can appear in offspring when crossing over happens between two linked gene locations.',
    'Why are genes farther apart on a chromosome more likely to be separated by crossing over?','There is a larger interval between them where a crossover can occur. For very far-apart genes the observed recombinant fraction can approach 50%.'],
  [14,'DNA Structure and Function','dna replication;dna polymerase;leading strand;lagging strand;okazaki fragments;dna repair',
    'DNA has two complementary strands. Each original strand serves as a template when DNA is copied. DNA polymerase builds new DNA 5′ to 3′, so one new strand at a fork is made in short pieces.',
    'Those short pieces on the lagging strand are Okazaki fragments. Ligase seals the remaining breaks in the backbone.',
    'Does the lagging strand get synthesized 3′ to 5′?','The lagging strand is synthesized 5′ to 3′ in pieces. The direction of the moving fork makes continuous synthesis possible only on the leading strand there.'],
  [15,'Genes and Proteins','protein synthesis;transcription;translation;codon;anticodon;genetic code',
    'Transcription copies a DNA template into RNA. During translation, a ribosome reads mRNA codons in order and tRNAs deliver amino acids. A start codon sets the reading frame and a stop codon ends translation.',
    'With the standard code, reading 5′-AUG GGU UAA-3′ gives methionine and glycine before the ribosome reaches a stop codon.',
    'Does a stop codon add an amino acid?','A release factor recognizes the stop codon and triggers release of the chain. The stop codon does not specify an amino acid.'],
  [16,'Gene Expression','gene regulation;differential gene expression;transcription factors;epigenetics;operon',
    'Cells can adjust how much of a gene product they make. Control can occur at transcription, RNA processing, translation, or after a protein is made. This lets cells with similar DNA carry out different jobs.',
    'A muscle cell and an intestinal cell use different combinations of genes. Their sets of proteins help explain their different shapes and functions.',
    'How can a cell increase the amount of a protein without changing its DNA sequence?','It can make more RNA from that gene, keep the RNA available longer, or translate more of it.'],
  [17,'Biotechnology and Genomics','dna evidence;genomics;genome comparisons;gel electrophoresis interpretation;biotechnology',
    'A genome is an organism’s full set of genetic material. Genomics compares many sequences or regions at once. Evidence from a DNA pattern can support a hypothesis about relatedness when the comparison includes appropriate controls.',
    'In a standard comparison of DNA bands, a reference lane gives sizes for the sample bands. Agreement in band position means fragments are similar in size.',
    'Do matching band positions by themselves prove that two DNA fragments have identical sequences?','They support similar fragment sizes. Different sequences can have the same length, so sequence identity needs additional evidence.'],
  [18,'Evolution and the Origin of Species','natural selection;adaptation;speciation;reproductive isolation;allopatric;prezygotic',
    'Natural selection changes the frequency of inherited traits when individuals differ in their contribution to the next generation. Speciation can follow when barriers reduce gene flow between populations.',
    'A shift in breeding season can prevent two populations from mating. This is temporal isolation, a barrier that acts before fertilization.',
    'Is a sterile hybrid an example of a prezygotic or a postzygotic barrier?','Postzygotic. A zygote formed and developed, but the resulting hybrid cannot reproduce successfully.'],
  [19,'The Evolution of Populations','population genetics;genetic drift;gene flow;hardy weinberg;allele frequency;founder effect',
    'Evolution can be measured as a change in allele frequency across generations. Selection can favor some variants, drift changes frequencies by chance, and migration can bring in new alleles. Hardy–Weinberg gives expected genotype proportions under a defined set of assumptions.',
    'For a two-allele gene, knowing p and q lets you predict the heterozygote fraction as 2pq at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium.',
    'If p = 0.7 and q = 0.3, what fraction is expected to be heterozygous at equilibrium?','2 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.42, or 42%.'],
  [20,'Phylogenies and the History of Life','phylogeny;cladogram;tree of life;common ancestor;clade;mass extinction',
    'A phylogenetic tree is a hypothesis about ancestry. Each branching point represents a shared ancestor. Fossils and molecular evidence help researchers connect such trees to events in the history of life.',
    'Rotating branches around a node changes the layout of the drawing. The descendant groups still share the same branching point.',
    'On a tree, how do you decide which two species are more closely related?','Find their most recent common ancestor. The pair sharing the more recent one is more closely related, regardless of how near their labels appear.'],
  [21,'Viruses','virus structure;viral particle;capsid;viruses vs cells',
    'A virus typically consists of genetic material inside a protein coat called a capsid. Some also have a lipid envelope. Viruses depend on cells to make new viral particles. Their structure and dependence on cells help distinguish them from bacteria.',
    'A bacterial cell has ribosomes for making proteins. A viral particle lacks that cellular machinery.',
    'Which structure surrounds the genetic material in a typical virus?','The protein capsid. Some viruses also have a lipid envelope outside the capsid.'],
  [22,'Prokaryotes: Bacteria and Archaea','bacteria and archaea;prokaryotes;bacterial ecology;archaeal membranes',
    'Bacteria and archaea are different domains whose cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus. They differ in features such as membrane chemistry. Prokaryotes carry out many ecological jobs, including breaking down material and cycling nutrients.',
    'Prokaryotes can live in soil, oceans, and animal digestive systems. Their way of obtaining energy varies widely.',
    'Does word prokaryote mean bacterium?','It includes both bacteria and archaea. The term describes cellular organization rather than one domain.'],
  [23,'Protists','protists;algae;microbial eukaryotes;protist diversity',
    'Protist is a practical label for many eukaryotes spread across the tree of life. Their ways of getting energy can include photosynthesis, consuming other organisms, or both.',
    'A photosynthetic alga and a cell that feeds on bacteria can both be called protists. Their shared label does not establish close ancestry.',
    'Why can you not identify all protists by looking for one way of getting food?','They include many lineages with different nutritional strategies.'],
  [24,'Fungi','fungi;fungal nutrition;hyphae;mycelium;mycorrhizae',
    'Many fungi release enzymes outside their bodies and absorb the resulting small molecules. A network of threads called hyphae is a mycelium. Fungi are important as decomposers and as partners of other organisms.',
    'In a mycorrhizal partnership, fungal threads can help a plant take up mineral nutrients, and the plant supplies the fungus with carbon compounds.',
    'How do many fungi obtain nutrients from leaf litter?','They break down material outside their cells and absorb smaller products.'],
  [25,'Seedless Plants','seedless plants;mosses;ferns;bryophytes;alternation of generations',
    'Land plants alternate between a haploid gametophyte and a diploid sporophyte. A moss’s leafy stage is usually the gametophyte. The fern fronds that are easiest to see belong to the sporophyte.',
    'Spore-producing structures on a fern sporophyte make haploid spores by meiosis. A spore can grow into a gametophyte by mitosis.',
    'Which plant generation produces gametes?','The haploid gametophyte makes gametes. The diploid sporophyte makes spores.'],
  [26,'Seed Plants','seed plants;gymnosperm;angiosperm;gymnosperms;angiosperms;plant diversity ii',
    'Pollen carries a male gametophyte, while a seed protects a developing sporophyte embryo. Gymnosperm seeds develop without a surrounding fruit. Flowering plants enclose their ovules in ovaries that commonly mature into fruits.',
    'Compare a pine seed on a cone scale with seeds inside a tomato. The tomato develops from a flower’s ovary.',
    'How does a pollen grain differ from a seed?','Pollen contains the male gametophyte that helps deliver sperm. A seed contains an embryo already formed after fertilization in the typical sexual cycle.'],
  [27,'Introduction to Animal Diversity','animal diversity;animal body plans;germ layers;symmetry;animal classification',
    'Animal groups can be compared by symmetry, embryonic tissues, development, and genetic ancestry. Similar-looking traits can evolve independently, so diagnoses combine several lines of evidence.',
    'A sea star adult has radial organization, yet its larva has bilateral symmetry. Comparing life stages can reveal relationships that the adult’s appearance alone hides.',
    'Does an adult sea star’s symmetry determine its entire evolutionary placement?','No. Its larval organization and other developmental and genetic evidence also matter.'],
  [28,'Invertebrates','invertebrate diversity;animal phyla;arthropods;mollusks;echinoderms;cnidarians;annelids',
    'Invertebrates include diverse animal groups. Jointed appendages are a clue for arthropods, stinging cells identify cnidarians, and a water vascular system is characteristic of echinoderms.',
    'A crab and a beetle have very different shapes. Both have jointed appendages and an exoskeleton that is shed during growth.',
    'Which group does a crab belong to on the evidence in this example?','Arthropods. Jointed appendages and a molted exoskeleton are useful clues.'],
  [29,'Vertebrates','vertebrate clades;vertebrates;chordate traits;vertebrate milestones;amniotic egg',
    'Chordates have a notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits or pouches, and a post-anal tail at some point in development. Vertebrates are a chordate lineage. Major branches are identified by shared derived traits such as jaws and limbs with digits.',
    'On a vertebrate tree, birds fall within the reptile lineage. Their wings and feathers are specialized features of that branch.',
    'If a chordate has a notochord, does that prove it is a vertebrate?','No. A notochord is shared beyond vertebrates. Some chordates, such as lancelets, lack vertebrae.'],
  [30,'Plant Form and Physiology','plant form;plant growth;meristem;xylem;phloem;transpiration;plant transport',
    'Roots, stems, and leaves contain tissues suited to different jobs. Apical meristems lengthen roots and shoots. Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals, while phloem distributes sugars from sources to sinks.',
    'During active growth, mature leaves can be sugar sources and a developing fruit a sugar sink.',
    'Which transport tissue supplies sugar to that developing fruit?','Phloem. Mature leaves load sugars that can be delivered to tissue using or storing them.'],
  [31,'Soil and Plant Nutrition','soil and plant nutrition;plant minerals;root nutrition;nitrogen fixation',
    'Plants use light to make organic molecules and need mineral nutrients from their environment. Soil chemistry and root associations influence which nutrients are available.',
    'Nitrogen-fixing microbes convert atmospheric nitrogen into compounds that can enter living systems. Some plants benefit through partnerships with those microbes.',
    'Why can added water alone fail to help a plant with a mineral deficiency?','The deficient mineral is still in short supply. Water can move dissolved nutrients, but it does not replace them.'],
  [32,'Plant Reproduction','plant reproduction;pollination;double fertilization;flowering plant reproduction;seed formation',
    'Pollination moves pollen to the structure where it can germinate. Fertilization occurs when gametes unite. In flowering plants, two sperm are involved in separate fusion events that lead to the embryo and endosperm.',
    'After fertilization, the ovule becomes a seed. The ovary usually develops into part or all of the fruit.',
    'Has fertilization occurred as soon as pollen lands on the stigma?','Pollination has occurred. Fertilization still requires delivery of sperm and gamete fusion.'],
  [33,'The Animal Body: Basic Form and Function','homeostasis;animal tissues;animal form and function;negative feedback;thermoregulation',
    'Animals organize cells into tissues and organs. Homeostasis keeps internal conditions within workable limits. In negative feedback, a response counteracts the disturbance that triggered it.',
    'When a person warms up, sweating can help transfer heat through evaporation.',
    'How does sweating illustrate negative feedback?','Rising temperature triggers a response that can lower temperature. The response counters the original change.'],
  [34,'Animal Nutrition and the Digestive System','animal nutrition;intracellular digestion;extracellular digestion;digestive system;absorption',
    'Digestion breaks food down into molecules the body can absorb. Intracellular digestion takes place inside cells. Extracellular digestion occurs in a cavity or tract outside the cells that perform the absorption.',
    'Food can be broken down in the intestine before its nutrients cross the intestinal lining into the body.',
    'Where does extracellular digestion occur in an animal with a digestive tract?','In the tract lumen. Cells can then absorb the resulting smaller molecules.'],
  [35,'The Nervous System','nervous system;neuron;action potential;synapse;neurotransmitter',
    'A neuron uses changes in membrane voltage to carry signals. Many neurons communicate with the next cell by releasing a chemical at a synapse. Groups of neurons coordinate sensation, processing, and response.',
    'An action potential travels along an axon. At a chemical synapse the outgoing signal can trigger release of a neurotransmitter.',
    'In this pathway, where does the signal switch from electrical to chemical?','At the chemical synapse, where the arriving action potential can trigger neurotransmitter release.'],
  [36,'Sensory Systems','sensory systems;sensory receptors;photoreceptor;mechanoreceptor;sensory transduction',
    'Sensory receptors turn a stimulus into a signal the nervous system can process. Different receptor types respond to stimuli such as light, mechanical force, or dissolved chemicals.',
    'In hearing, movement inside the inner ear bends hair-cell projections. The mechanical movement changes the cell’s signaling.',
    'What kind of physical stimulus starts the signal in a hearing hair cell?','Mechanical movement. These hair cells are mechanoreceptors.'],
  [37,'The Endocrine System','endocrine system;endocrine signaling;hormones;blood glucose feedback',
    'Endocrine cells release hormones into the bloodstream. A hormone changes the activity of cells with receptors for it. Feedback often helps regulate hormone release.',
    'After a meal raises blood glucose, insulin signaling can help the body take up and store glucose and can reduce the amount released by the liver.',
    'Why does the same hormone in the bloodstream not affect every cell in the same way?','Cells differ in which receptors they have and what those receptors do after the hormone binds.'],
  [38,'The Musculoskeletal System','musculoskeletal system;muscle contraction;sliding filament;skeletal muscle;sarcomere',
    'Skeletons give the body support and provide a structure muscles can pull on. In skeletal muscle, actin and myosin slide past one another as a sarcomere shortens. Calcium and ATP help regulate and power the process.',
    'Bending the elbow involves forces from muscles on different sides of the joint. A shortening muscle pulls on the bone through a tendon.',
    'Do the actin and myosin filaments get shorter during a typical contraction?','Their overlap changes as they slide. The sarcomere shortens while the filaments keep approximately the same lengths.'],
  [39,'The Respiratory System','respiratory system;gas exchange;alveolar ventilation;alveoli;respiration and breathing',
    'Ventilation moves air or water across a gas-exchange surface. Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse according to partial-pressure gradients. Circulation then carries gases between that surface and the tissues.',
    'Minute ventilation includes every inhaled breath. Alveolar ventilation accounts for the volume that never reaches the gas-exchanging region.',
    'Why do lungs use many small alveoli?','Many alveoli provide a large total surface area for gas exchange. Their thin walls also shorten the diffusion distance.'],
  [40,'The Circulatory System','circulatory system;pulmonary circulation;systemic circulation;cardiac output;blood vessels',
    'Circulation moves materials through the body. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins return it, and capillaries are sites of exchange. In mammals the pulmonary pathway connects heart and lungs, and the systemic pathway reaches other tissues.',
    'The pulmonary artery carries relatively oxygen-poor blood from the heart toward the lungs.',
    'Does oxygen content determine whether a blood vessel is an artery?','Blood flow direction does. The pulmonary artery carries blood away from the heart.'],
  [41,'Osmotic Regulation and Excretion','osmoregulation;excretion;nephron;kidney filtration;nitrogenous waste',
    'Osmoregulation balances water and dissolved substances, while excretion removes metabolic wastes. A nephron filters fluid from the blood and then changes that fluid through reabsorption and secretion.',
    'Reabsorbing a useful molecule moves it from the nephron fluid back toward the blood.',
    'Which process returns filtered glucose to the bloodstream under typical physiology?','Tubular reabsorption. Filtration put the glucose in the nephron fluid and reabsorption returns it.'],
  [42,'The Immune System','immune system;innate immunity;adaptive immunity;antibodies;immune memory',
    'Innate immune defenses recognize broad patterns and can act quickly. Adaptive responses use cells that recognize particular targets. Some of those cells remain as memory cells after the initial response.',
    'After an earlier encounter, memory cells can help the adaptive system respond faster to the same target.',
    'Why can a second exposure produce a faster adaptive response?','Specific memory cells formed during the earlier response can become active and expand sooner.'],
  [43,'Animal Reproduction and Development','animal reproduction;animal development;cleavage;gastrulation;organogenesis',
    'During sexual reproduction, gametes fuse to form a zygote. Early cell divisions produce a multicellular embryo. Gastrulation rearranges cells into layers that contribute to different tissues.',
    'Cleavage partitions the early embryo into more cells. It can occur with little overall increase in embryo size.',
    'Which process establishes the major embryonic tissue layers?','Gastrulation. Earlier cleavage divisions generate cells that can be rearranged.'],
  [44,'Ecology and the Biosphere','biosphere;biomes;ecology levels;ecology and the biosphere;species distribution',
    'Ecologists study interactions at scales ranging from individual organisms to the biosphere. Climate and other abiotic factors shape where species occur. Species interactions can limit distributions too.',
    'A question about all individuals of one species in a pond concerns population ecology. A question about their predator and prey relationships also brings in the surrounding community.',
    'What changes when an ecologist goes from studying a community to studying its ecosystem?','The ecosystem question includes the community’s exchanges with its nonliving setting, such as water, soil, and energy inputs.'],
  [45,'Population and Community Ecology','population growth;community ecology;carrying capacity;competition;survivorship curves;mark recapture',
    'Population ecology studies the size and change of a group of one species. Logistic growth slows as a population approaches carrying capacity. Community ecology considers how populations of different species interact.',
    'If a growing population approaches carrying capacity while conditions stay fixed, the logistic model predicts its net growth rate will decline.',
    'What does the logistic model predict at N = K?','Zero net growth. The factor (K − N)/K is zero. Individuals can still be born or die.'],
  [46,'Ecosystems','energy flow;food webs;trophic levels;ten percent rule;biogeochemical cycles;ecosystem productivity',
    'Energy enters many ecosystems when producers capture sunlight. At each feeding step, only some energy becomes new biomass available to the next level. Matter such as carbon moves through reusable pools.',
    'At 10% transfer efficiency, 2,000 kJ of producer production would support about 200 kJ of new primary-consumer production. Real efficiencies vary.',
    'Using 10% again, how much production would reach the next consumer level?','About 20 kJ. The second transfer starts from the 200 kJ already available to it.'],

    .replace(/\bdiffrence\b/g,'difference')
    .replace(/\b(?:expontential|exponetial|exponental)\b/g,'exponential')
    .replace(/\b(?:logisitic|logisitcal)\b/g,'logistic')
    .replace(/\b(?:gametophite|gametophyt)\b/g,'gametophyte')
    .replace(/\b(?:sporophite|sporophyt)\b/g,'sporophyte')
    .replace(/\b(?:hypotomic|isotomic|hypertonc)\b/g,value=>({hypotomic:'hypotonic',isotomic:'isotonic',hypertonc:'hypertonic'})[value])
    .replace(/[’']/g,'').replace(/[‐‑–—]|(?<=[a-z])-(?=[a-z])/g,' ').replace(/\s+/g,' ').trim();
}

function identify(query){
  if(/\b(?:tonicity|hypertonic|hypotonic|isotonic|plasmolys\w*|turgor|aquaporin\w*|water potential)\b/.test(query))return 'tonicity';
  if(/\b(?:red blood cells?|rbc|plant cells?|potato)\b/.test(query)&&/\b(?:osmosis|water|saline|salty|sucrose|swells?|bursts?|shrink\w*|mass gain|mass loss)\b/.test(query))return 'tonicity';
  if(/\b(?:gametophyt\w*|sporophyt\w*|alternation of generations|sori|sorus)\b/.test(query))return 'generations';
  if(/\b(?:mosses|moss|ferns?|pines?)\b/.test(query)&&/\b(?:ploidy|haploid|diploid|gamete\w*|meiosis|fertiliz\w*|spores?)\b/.test(query))return 'generations';
  if(/\b(?:logistic growth|carrying capacity)\b/.test(query)||/\bexponential\b.*\blogistic\b|\blogistic\b.*\bexponential\b/.test(query))return 'growth';
  if(/\b(?:atp|fadh2|nadh|proton gradient|etc)\b/.test(query)&&/\b(?:aerobic|glucose|glycolysis|fadh2|shuttle|oxidative phosphorylation|atp synthase|electron transport|citric acid|fermentation|substrate level)\b/.test(query))return 'atp';
  return null;
}

const number='([+−-]?(?:\\d{1,3}(?:,\\d{3})+|\\d+)(?:\\.\\d+)?|[+−-]?\\.\\d+)';
const parseNumber=value=>value===undefined?undefined:Number(value.replace(/,/g,'').replace('−','-'));
const format=value=>Number(value.toPrecision(8)).toLocaleString('en-US',{maximumFractionDigits:10});
const populationAssignments={
  N:new RegExp('\\b(?:N|(?:current |initial )?population(?: size)?)\\s*(?:=|:|is(?: now)?|of|has)\\s*'+number,'i'),
  r:new RegExp('\\b(?:r|(?:intrinsic |per capita )?(?:growth )?rate)\\s*(?:=|:|is|of)\\s*'+number+'\\s*(%)?','i'),
  K:new RegExp('\\b(?:K|carrying capacity)\\s*(?:=|:|is|of)\\s*'+number,'i')
};

function populationValues(input){
  const N=parseNumber(input.match(populationAssignments.N)?.[1]);
  const K=parseNumber(input.match(populationAssignments.K)?.[1]);
  const rate=input.match(populationAssignments.r);
  const rateValue=parseNumber(rate?.[1]);
  const r=rate?.[2]==='%'?rateValue/100:rateValue;
  const time=input.match(/\b(?:per\s+|\/\s*|each\s+)(year|month|week|day|hour|minute|second)s?\b/i)?.[1]?.toLowerCase();
  return Object.fromEntries(Object.entries({N,K,r,time}).filter(([,value])=>value!==undefined));
}

const defaultPopulation={N:200,r:0.1,K:1000,time:'year',illustrative:true};

function populationWork(values,compare=false){
  const {N,r,K,time}=values;
  const unit='individuals per '+(time??'unit of time');
  const exponential=r*N;
  const fraction=(K-N)/K;
  const logistic=exponential*fraction;
  const fractionText=format(fraction);
  const isRounded=Number(fractionText.replaceAll(',',''))!==fraction;
  return {unit,exponential,fraction,logistic,steps:[
    'First calculate rN. '+format(r)+' × '+format(N)+' = '+format(exponential)+' '+unit+(compare?' under the exponential model.':'.'),
    'For logistic growth, the remaining fraction is ('+format(K)+' − '+format(N)+') / '+format(K)+(isRounded?' ≈ ':' = ')+fractionText+'.',
    'Multiply '+format(exponential)+' by '+(isRounded?'the exact fraction ('+format(K-N)+' / '+format(K)+')':fractionText)+' to get '+format(logistic)+' '+unit+'.'
  ]};
}

function populationAnswer(values,{example=false,compare=false,exponentialOnly=false}={}){
  const required=exponentialOnly?['N','r']:['N','r','K'];
  const missing=required.filter(name=>!Number.isFinite(values[name]));
  if(missing.length)return reply('growth','To work your numbers through, I still need '+missing.join(' and ')+'. N is the current population, r is the growth rate per individual per unit time, and K is the carrying capacity.',
    {intent:'clarify',formula:exponentialOnly?'dN/dt = rN':'dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K'});
  const {N,r,K,time}=values;
  if(N<0||!exponentialOnly&&K<=0)return reply('growth','Check the givens. A population size N must be zero or higher, and the logistic equation needs a positive carrying capacity K.',{intent:'clarify'});
  if(exponentialOnly){
    const total=r*N;
    return reply('growth','For this exponential model, multiply the rate per individual by the current population.',
      {intent:'worked',formula:'dN/dt = rN',steps:[format(r)+' × '+format(N)+' = '+format(total)+' individuals per '+(time??'unit of time')+'.']});
  }
  const work=populationWork(values,compare);
  const lead=example?topics.growth.text:(work.logistic<0?'Your population is decreasing at this instant in the logistic model.':'Here is the logistic growth rate for your numbers.');
  return reply('growth',lead,{intent:'worked',formula:compare?'Exponential dN/dt = rN. Logistic dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K.':'dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K',
    steps:work.steps,answer:format(work.logistic)+' '+work.unit+(compare?' (logistic), versus '+format(work.exponential)+' '+work.unit+' (exponential)':'')});
}

function growthContextual(query,values){
  const work=populationWork(values);
  const {N,K}=values;
  if(/\b(?:why\b.*\b(?:multip\w*|subtract\w*|divid\w*)|(?:where|how)\b.*\b(?:get|come from)|remaining fraction)\b/.test(query)
    ||/\b(?:fraction|multiply|divid\w*|logistic term)\b.*\b(?:k|capacity)\b/.test(query)){
    if(/\b(?:why\b.*\b(?:multiply|use)\b.*\b(?:r|n)\b|r\s*n)\b/.test(query)&&!/\b(?:fraction|k)\b/.test(query)){
      return reply('growth','r is the rate for one individual. Multiply it by all '+format(N)+' individuals to get '+format(work.exponential)+' '+work.unit+' before adjusting for crowding.');
    }
    return reply('growth','Start with the room left, K − N. In this example, '+format(K)+' − '+format(N)+' = '+format(K-N)+'. Divide that by K to express it as a fraction of the total capacity, '+format(work.fraction)+'. Multiplying rN by that fraction gives '+format(work.logistic)+' '+work.unit+'.',{steps:work.steps});
  }
  const guess=query.match(/\b(?:i got|my answer is|i found)\s*([−+]?(?:\d+(?:\.\d+)?|\.\d+))\b/);
  if(guess){
    const answer=parseNumber(guess[1]);
    if(Math.abs(answer-work.logistic)<1e-8)return reply('growth','Yes, '+format(answer)+' '+work.unit+' is the logistic rate. Your calculation used both the number of individuals and the fraction of capacity remaining.');
    if(Math.abs(answer-work.exponential)<1e-8)return reply('growth','You found rN, the exponential rate. For logistic growth, also multiply by the remaining-capacity fraction '+format(work.fraction)+'.',
      {question:'What do you get after that multiplication?',actions:[['Show that calculation','How did you get the logistic result?']]});
    return reply('growth','Let’s check each part of the calculation. Recompute the uncrowded rate rN, then compute (K − N)/K before multiplying the two results.',{steps:work.steps});
  }
  return null;
}

const glucoseNumber={one:1,two:2,three:3,four:4,five:5,six:6,seven:7,eight:8,nine:9,ten:10};
function glucoseAmount(query){
  const match=query.match(/\b(\d+|one|two|three|four|five|six|seven|eight|nine|ten)\s+(?:molecules?\s+of\s+)?glucose\b/);
  return match?Number(glucoseNumber[match[1]]??match[1]):undefined;
}

function scaleATP(amount,fermentation=false){
  if(!Number.isSafeInteger(amount*32)||amount<1)return null;
  const range=fermentation?'2 ATP / glucose':'30–32 ATP / glucose';
  const result=fermentation?format(2*amount):format(30*amount)+'–'+format(32*amount);
  const species=amount===1?'glucose molecule':'glucose molecules';
  return reply('atp','For '+format(amount)+' '+species+', the estimate is '+result+' ATP under '+(fermentation?'fermentation':'the aerobic respiration assumptions we used')+'.',
    {intent:'worked',steps:[format(amount)+' '+species+' × ('+range+') = '+result+' ATP.'+(fermentation?' The ATP comes from glycolysis.':' The two bounds use different estimates for the glycolysis NADH shuttle.')]});
}

function tonicityCalculation(query,input){
  const concentration=input.match(new RegExp(number+'\\s*(M|mM)\\b'));
  const volumeChange=query.match(/\b(swells?|swelling|shrinks?|shrunken|shrinking)\b/);
  if(!concentration||!volumeChange||!/\b(?:cell|interior|internal|inside)\b/.test(query))return null;
  const value=parseNumber(concentration[1]);
  if(value<0)return reply('tonicity','Check the concentration in the problem. A molar concentration can’t be negative.',{intent:'clarify'});
  const swelled=volumeChange[1].startsWith('sw');
  const outside=concentration[1]+' '+concentration[2];
  const relation=swelled?'higher':'lower';
  return reply('tonicity','The cell interior has a '+relation+' effective solute concentration than the '+outside+' solution, assuming sucrose stays outside and pressures were initially equal.',
    {intent:'worked',steps:['The cell '+(swelled?'swells, so net water entered.':'shrinks, so net water left.'),'Net water moved toward the side with the higher effective solute concentration. That puts the richer side '+(swelled?'inside':'outside')+' the cell.']});
}

export function createBiologyCoach(){
  let active=null,population=null,lastWorked=null,nextStep=0;
  function reset(){
    active=null;
    population=null;
    lastWorked=null;
    nextStep=0;
  }
  function remember(key,response){
    active=key;
    if(response.steps?.length){
      lastWorked=response.steps;
      nextStep=0;
    }
    return response;
  }
  function respond(raw,course=''){
    const input=String(raw??'').trim();
    if(!input||/^chem/i.test(course)||/^(?:new (?:problem|question|topic)|start over|forget (?:this|it|that))\b/i.test(input)){
      reset();
      return null;
    }
    const query=learnerText(input);
    const explicit=identify(query);
    const assignments=populationValues(input);
    const hasNumbers=['N','r','K'].filter(key=>assignments[key]!==undefined);
    const recognizedPopulation=hasNumbers.length>=2||
      hasNumbers.length===1&&active==='growth'&&/^(?:(?:and|ok(?:ay)?|what if|what about|now|assume|suppose|try|if|set|change) ){0,3}(?:n|r|k|(?:current |initial )?population|carrying capacity|(?:growth )?rate)\b/.test(query);
    const key=explicit??(recognizedPopulation?'growth':active);
    if(!key)return null;
    if(active!==key)reset();

    if(key==='growth'){
      if(hasNumbers.length&&(explicit==='growth'||recognizedPopulation)){
        const values={...population,...assignments};
        if(!assignments.time&&hasNumbers.includes('r')&&(hasNumbers.length>=2||population?.illustrative)){
          delete values.time;
        }
        if(hasNumbers.includes('r'))values.illustrative=false;
        const compare=/\bexponential\b/.test(query)&&/\blogistic\b/.test(query);
        const exponentialOnly=/\bexponential\b/.test(query)&&!/\blogistic\b/.test(query);
        const response=populationAnswer(values,{compare,exponentialOnly});
        if(response.intent==='worked'&&!exponentialOnly)population=values;
        return remember(key,response);
      }
      if(population){
        const response=growthContextual(query,population);
        if(response)return remember(key,response);
      }
    }
    if(key==='tonicity'){
      const response=tonicityCalculation(query,input);
      if(response)return remember(key,response);
    }
    if(key==='atp'){
      const amount=glucoseAmount(query);
      const fermentation=/\bfermentation\b/.test(query);
      if((amount>1||amount===1&&fermentation)&&!/\b(?:citric acid|krebs|glycolysis|electron transport|fadh2|nadh|payoff|invested)\b/.test(query)){
        const response=scaleATP(amount,fermentation);
        if(response)return remember(key,response);
      }
    }
    const branch=followups[key].find(([pattern])=>pattern.test(query));
    if(branch)return remember(key,reply(key,branch[1],branch[2]));

    if(active===key){
      if(/^(?:(?:ok(?:ay)?|and) )?(?:please )?(?:can i get |give me |i need |show me )?(?:a )?hint\b/.test(query)){
        return reply(key,hints[key],{question:checks[key],actions:[['Walk through the first step','Show me the first step']]});
      }
      if(/^(?:(?:ok(?:ay)?|and) )?(?:can you |please )?(?:show me (?:the )?first step|(?:what(?:s| is) (?:the )?)?next step|what next|then what)[?.! ]*$/.test(query)&&lastWorked?.length){
        if(/\bfirst\b/.test(query))nextStep=0;
        if(nextStep>=lastWorked.length)return reply(key,'That completes the walkthrough. Try checking your understanding with this question.',{question:checks[key]});
        const detail=lastWorked[nextStep++];
        return reply(key,detail,{actions:[['Next step','Next step'],['Give me a hint','Give me a hint']]});
      }
      if(/^(?:(?:ok(?:ay)?|and) )?(?:can you |could you |please )?(?:i (?:still )?dont (?:understand|get it)|why|(?:can you )?explain (?:this|that|it)(?: again)?|break (?:it|this|that) down|(?:say|explain) (?:it|that) (?:more simply|in simple (?:terms|words)))[?.! ]*$/.test(query)){
        return reply(key,simple[key],{question:checks[key]});
      }
    }
    if(!explicit){
      reset();
      return null;
    }
    if(key==='growth'){
      population={...defaultPopulation};
      return remember(key,populationAnswer(population,{example:true,compare:true}));
    }
    return remember(key,reply(key,topics[key].text,{intent:'definition',steps:topics[key].steps}));
  }
  return {respond,reset};
}

export function buildExamHint(item) {
  const key=item.chapterId==='measurements'&&/in liters/i.test(item.question)?'measurements-volume':item.chapterId;
  const guide=hints[key];
  const clueList=guide?.clues.flatMap(([pattern,meaning])=>{
    const match=item.question.match(pattern);
    return match?[{quote:match[0],meaning}]:[];
  })??[];
  const target=item.question.match(/\b((?:What|Which|How many|How much|How does|Determine|Calculate)[^?]*\?)[.\s]*$/i)?.[1];
  if(!clueList.length&&target)clueList.push({quote:target,meaning:'This is the requested result. Use the earlier details to decide how to reach it.'});
  return {
    clues:clueList,
    start:guide?.start??'Write down what the question asks you to identify, explain, or calculate.',
    method:guide?.method??'Separate the observations from assumptions. Use the relationship or comparison that connects them to the target.',
    check:guide?.check??'Check that the choice explains all the stated evidence.',
    formula:guide?.formula
  };
}

const byId = new Map(chemistryChapterEntries.map(card => [card.id, card]));
const words = input => String(input).normalize('NFKC').toLowerCase()
  .replace(/[’']/g, '').replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, ' ').trim().replace(/\s+/g, ' ');

export function chemistryChapterFollowup(topicId, input) {
  const card = byId.get(topicId);
  if (!card) return null;
  const text = words(input);
  const match = card.followups.find(item => item.aliases.some(alias =>
    ` ${text} `.includes(` ${words(alias)} `)));
  const reason = /^(?:and )?why (?:does (?:that|it) matter|is (?:that|it) important|do we need (?:that|it))$/.test(text);
  const answer = match?.answer ?? (reason ? card.why : null);
  return answer ? {topic: card.id, title: card.title, text: answer, links: [card.source]} : null;
}
